reference.source: Apley & Solomon / standard sports medicine references
clinicalPearls: The typical mechanism is an inversion and plantarflexion injury damaging the lateral ligament complex, with the anterior talofibular ligament injured first
Sprains are graded from mild ligament stretch (grade I) through partial tear (grade II) to complete rupture with instability (grade III)
Use the Ottawa ankle rules to decide on radiographs and reduce unnecessary imaging
Always palpate the proximal fibula, base of the fifth metatarsal, navicular, and medial malleolus to avoid missing associated fractures
A high ankle (syndesmotic) sprain from an external rotation injury causes pain above the joint line, is confirmed by the squeeze and external rotation tests, and has a longer recovery
Marked medial-sided pain or a positive external rotation test raises concern for a Maisonneuve injury with a proximal fibular fracture
Early functional management with relative rest, compression, elevation, and progressive weight-bearing and mobilisation is preferred over prolonged immobilisation
Rehabilitation with proprioceptive and balance training and peroneal strengthening reduces the risk of recurrent sprains and chronic instability
Most sprains recover well, but a significant minority develop chronic instability or persistent symptoms if inadequately rehabilitated
reference.pathophysiology: An ankle sprain is a ligamentous injury, most often to the lateral complex (anterior talofibular, calcaneofibular, and posterior talofibular ligaments), caused by forced inversion. Excessive load tears collagen fibres, causing bleeding, swelling, and loss of mechanical restraint. Syndesmotic (high ankle) sprains involve the distal tibiofibular ligaments from external rotation. Impaired ligament healing and proprioceptive deficits can lead to mechanical and functional instability.
additionalDifferentials: Lateral malleolus, fifth metatarsal base, or other foot/ankle fracture
Peroneal tendon subluxation, tear, or dislocation
additionalInvestigations: Apply the Ottawa ankle and foot rules to select patients for plain radiographs
Weight-bearing or stress radiographs if syndesmotic disruption or instability is suspected
MRI for suspected osteochondral lesions, occult injury, or persistent symptoms
Ultrasound to assess peroneal tendon and ligament integrity
Consider proximal fibula imaging when a Maisonneuve injury is suspected
redFlags: Inability to bear weight and bony tenderness meeting Ottawa criteria, indicating possible fracture
Proximal fibular tenderness suggesting a Maisonneuve fracture
Gross instability, deformity, or neurovascular compromise
Persistent locking, catching, or effusion suggesting an osteochondral lesion
reference.prognosis: Most low-grade lateral sprains recover within weeks with functional treatment, but up to a third develop residual symptoms or chronic instability; syndesmotic injuries recover more slowly and unstable injuries may require surgery.
pitfalls: Missing associated fractures such as the fifth metatarsal base or a Maisonneuve injury
Failing to identify a syndesmotic sprain and underestimating recovery time
Prolonged immobilisation leading to stiffness and deconditioning
Omitting proprioceptive rehabilitation, increasing the risk of recurrent sprains
references: Apley & Solomon's System of Orthopaedics and Fractures
management: Manage the acute injury with relative rest, ice, compression, elevation, and early protected weight-bearing as pain allows
Provide analgesia with paracetamol or non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs
Begin early functional rehabilitation with range-of-motion, proprioceptive and balance training, and progressive strengthening
Use external support such as bracing or taping to stabilise the joint and reduce re-injury
Treat syndesmotic (high ankle) sprains with longer protected weight-bearing or immobilisation and refer for orthopaedic review if unstable
Refer for surgical opinion in complete unstable rupture, Maisonneuve injury, or associated fracture
Follow up persistent or recurrent instability with continued physiotherapy and consider ligament reconstruction
